notes.meaning: Nineveh is called a city of blood because of its constant violence, murder, and greed. The Assyrians built their empire by brutally robbing other nations and never stopped hunting for more victims. God announces a sorrowful doom over this city because of its cruel deeds and endless lies.

The prophet paints a vivid picture of an invading army crashing into Nineveh. The air fills with cracking whips, rattling wheels, galloping horses, and flashing weapons. The battle leaves behind huge mounds of bodies, so crowded that running soldiers stumble over the dead.

Nineveh acted like an alluring prostitute who charmed other nations into ruin. The Assyrians used tempting promises, trade agreements, and idolatrous rituals to draw neighbouring peoples under their control and enslave them. God held the empire guilty for using deceit and spiritual corruption to prey upon weaker countries.

The Lord of Hosts announces directly that He has become Nineveh's enemy. Just as unfaithful women were once publicly exposed and humiliated in the ancient world, God will strip away Assyria's rich coverings and defenses. The proud capital will be left totally naked and disgraced before the kingdoms of the earth.

God promises to throw disgusting filth at the city and treat it with utter contempt. In Bible times, disgraced criminals were made a public spectacle and pelted with garbage and mud. In the same way, the Lord will turn proud Nineveh into a shameful sight for all to mock.

Anyone who looks upon ruined Nineveh will pull back in shock and disgust. No one will shed a tear or comfort her, because she had shown no pity to anyone else in her days of power. The fallen capital will be left completely alone in her desolation.

Nahum challenges Nineveh to consider whether it is any safer than Thebes, the historic and mighty capital of Upper Egypt. Thebes seemed unconquerable because it was surrounded by the waters of the Nile like a protective sea. Yet even those grand water defenses could not save it from being destroyed.

Thebes relied on vast military alliances to guarantee her security. Ethiopia and the rest of Egypt gave her endless supplies of soldiers, while Put and Libya guarded her as strong allies. Yet human partners and massive armies were not enough to hold back judgment.

Even with all its power, Thebes was conquered and its citizens marched away into exile. Invading soldiers brutally dashed Egyptian infants against the street stones and rolled dice to divide the city's leaders as slaves. Nineveh had helped inflict that very horror on Egypt, and now the same brutal fate was coming for her.

Nineveh will be forced to drink from the cup of God's wrath until she staggers like a drunkard. Her terrified leaders and people will run to hide from their enemies and look everywhere for shelter. The once fearless world power will be completely helpless to save itself.

All the fortified border outposts guarding Nineveh are compared to fig trees loaded with early ripe figs. As soon as the branches are lightly shaken, the ripe fruit drops effortlessly into the eater's mouth. In the exact same way, Assyria's strongholds will fall to the invaders at the first assault.

Assyria's fierce soldiers will lose their nerve and become as timid and panic-stricken as frightened civilians. The fortified mountain passes and river gates will swing wide open to the attackers. Blazing fire will burn right through the heavy wooden gate bars that used to lock enemies out.

The prophet sarcastically tells the Ninevites to get ready for the coming siege. He tells them to fill their water reservoirs, stomp the mud, and fire the brick kilns to build emergency walls. Yet this taunting advice shows that human preparations are completely useless against God's decree.

Right inside their strong defenses, fire will burn the Assyrians up and enemy swords will cut them down like hungry locusts. The prophet mocks them by urging them to multiply their troops into vast swarms. No matter how large their numbers grow, the judgment will eat them up just as fast as locusts strip a field.

Nineveh had drawn so many merchants to its wealthy markets that they seemed to outnumber the stars in the sky. But like a swarm of young locusts that strips a field and suddenly takes flight, these traders will pack up their goods and scatter. When the crisis hits, all the wealth and foreign traders will disappear.

The city's commanders and royal officials are compared to locusts resting on a cold stone wall. When it is chilly, locusts stay numb and motionless, but the moment the morning sun warms them, they fly off and vanish into the sky. In the exact same way, Assyria's proud officers will flee when danger heats up, leaving no trace behind.

Nahum directly addresses the king of Assyria, warning him that his 'shepherds,' or royal leaders, are slumbering in death. With no officers left to direct them, the ordinary people are scattered across the mountains like lost sheep. There is no one left to round them up or lead the kingdom anymore.

There is no cure for Assyria's broken condition; the empire's death blow is final. When other nations hear the news of Nineveh's ruin, they will clap their hands with relief and joy. Because everyone had suffered under Assyria's unending cruelty, the whole world celebrates its fall.
